How can I tell when a property last got a new roof or HVAC system from its permit history?

By PermitsByCounty Research Team · Published November 9, 2026 · Guides & Answers

QUICK ANSWER

Pull the full permit history for the address, newest first, and find two lines: the newest closed re-roof or replacement line, and the newest closed mechanical line for a full HVAC change-out. A permit history roof replacement line gives you the best public date for the roof — use its final inspection date when it has one, and the issue date when it does not. Do the same for HVAC, then judge what is left against normal life: about 20 years for 3-tab asphalt shingles and 30 for architectural, 7 to 15 years for central air conditioning, and 15 to 25 years for a furnace, per InterNACHI’s chart, checked November 9, 2026. If no replacement line shows up, you have proved only that no replacement was recorded — not that the system is original.

TL;DR — the whole post in 20 seconds

  • Two lines date the two big systems: the newest closed roof replacement line, and the newest closed mechanical line for a full change-out.
  • Repairs do not reset the clock. A patch or a new fan motor is upkeep, not a new system.
  • Judge the date against normal life: 20 to 30 years for asphalt shingles, 7 to 15 for central air, 15 to 25 for a furnace.
  • No line is not a verdict. The permit may sit in a paper file somewhere. Some jobs never needed one, and some work was done with none.

Where does a permit history roof replacement show up?

In the same address search you would use for any other work. Pull every permit tied to the address or the parcel number, sorted by date, and read the whole list — not just the building permits. A big job often leaves several lines, one per trade. The roof line usually sits under a building permit, with words like re-roof, roof replacement, or tear-off in the description. The HVAC line usually sits under a mechanical permit, because heating and cooling work is mechanical work in most permit systems. LegalClarity’s permit-reading guide sorts it the same way: a permit’s type is building, electrical, mechanical, or plumbing, and a big job generates separate permits for different trades.

“Permit history is a strong proxy. You can see when the roof was last replaced, whether the HVAC or water heater has been updated, and whether renovations were permitted”

The proxy this whole method rests on — United States · Properties data page, checked November 9, 2026

Source: Shovels, Properties Data · Date pulled: November 9, 2026

Shovels, which sells property data built from permits, tells buyers to check the age of the roof, HVAC, or water heater from past permits. And that really is the whole method — you read dated public records of the work itself instead of guessing from a listing photo.

Cities keep the fields you need. Austin’s issued-permits dataset carries a permit type description, a work class, a detailed description of the work, and the issue date for every permit. Other cities name the fields differently, but the same four facts are there.

Austin’s Issued Construction Permits dataset covers Building, Electrical, Mechanical, and Plumbing Permits and includes issue date, description of work, square footage, and valuation for each permit; its 68 columns include Permit Type Desc, Work Class, Description, and Issued Date

The fields that date a system — City of Austin, Texas · Dataset page checked November 9, 2026; dataset last updated November 9, 2026

Source: City of Austin Open Data, Issued Construction Permits · Date pulled: November 9, 2026

How do you read a roof line without fooling yourself?

Start with what should be there at all. A full re-roof is the kind of work most places want on a permit. LegalClarity’s guide lists roofing as full re-roofing or structural repairs to the roof system, and puts cosmetic work and minor repairs on the no-permit side. So a real replacement normally leaves a line. A small patch job normally does not, and its absence tells you nothing.

Work that typically requires a permit includes mechanical systems — new or replacement HVAC, water heaters, and ductwork — and roofing — full re-roofing or structural repairs to the roof system; cosmetic updates and minor repairs that do not alter the structure or its systems generally do not

Which roof and HVAC jobs normally get a permit — United States · Permit lookup guide, checked November 9, 2026

Source: LegalClarity, How to Look Up Construction Permits Online and In Person · Date pulled: November 9, 2026

Then sort the roof lines into two piles. Replacement pile: re-roof, roof replacement, tear-off and re-roof, new roof, a description that names the whole roof. Repair pile: roof repair, leak repair, patch, flashing, vent boot, partial slope. Only the newest line in the replacement pile starts your clock.

Size is your cross-check. A replacement line usually carries a valuation in line with a whole roof job and, in datasets like Austin’s, a square footage that sounds like the whole house. A repair line carries a small valuation. If a line says “roof” but the value looks like a few hundred dollars, read it as a repair until the description proves otherwise.

Watch for the overlay trap. Some re-roofs add a new layer over the old one instead of tearing it off. The date still counts, but write the word overlay next to it — the old layer is still under it, and your inspector should know. And use the right year zero: if a house was built in 2009 and has no roof line at all, the working assumption is a 2009 roof. An assumption, not a record — hold it loosely.

How do you read an HVAC line?

Look under mechanical. A full system swap is normally filed as a mechanical permit, and the description is where it shows: change-out, change out, replace furnace, replace AC, new HVAC system, install heat pump, or a paired line the same week for a furnace and a condenser together. Austin even tracks change-out as its own work class, and it is a busy one.

In March 2026, Austin issued 4,851 permits across all trade types; mechanical permits were 934 of them (19.3%), and permits in the Change Out work class were 671 (13.8%)

Change-outs are their own readable slice — City of Austin, Texas · March 2026

Source: BCAR DATA, Austin Building Permit Report, March 2026, compiled from City of Austin public permit records · Date pulled: November 9, 2026

Sort the mechanical lines the same way you sorted the roof. Replacement words: change-out, replace, new system, new furnace, new condenser, new heat pump. Repair words: service call, capacitor, blower motor, coil cleaning, refrigerant, control board. A repair can keep an old system alive for years. It just doesn’t make the system any younger.

Date the two halves apart. Most homes heat with one unit and cool with another, and they rarely die in the same year. A 2019 line for a furnace and a 2014 line for a condenser mean a mid-life furnace and an older air conditioner, not “HVAC from about 2016.” Write both dates down separately. A heat pump is the exception: one unit does both jobs, so one change-out line dates the whole system. A ductwork line is not a system date either — new ducts on an old furnace leave you with an old furnace. Note it, and keep looking for the equipment line itself.

Which date do you trust — applied, issued, or final?

The final inspection date, when you can find it. The application date just shows when someone asked, and the issue date is the day the city said yes. Trust the final date instead — that is when the city came back, checked the finished work, and signed it off, so it sits closest to the day the work was actually done.

LegalClarity’s reading guide states the statuses plainly. “Issued” means the permit was approved but work may still be in progress. “Finaled” or “closed” means the work passed all required inspections. “Expired” means the work was not finished within the allowed time. So a finaled line is the date to write down. An issued line with no inspection after it may or may not have been finished — treat that date as soft, and ask for the contractor’s invoice before you rely on it.

“Issued” means the permit was approved but work may still be in progress; “Finaled” or “closed” means the work passed all required inspections and the permit is complete; “Expired” means the work was not finished within the allowed timeframe

What the status line means — United States · Permit lookup guide, checked November 9, 2026

Source: LegalClarity, How to Look Up Construction Permits Online and In Person · Date pulled: November 9, 2026

An expired roof or HVAC permit is a flag, not a date. If the last roof line is expired and no later replacement line follows it, the work behind it may never have been finished or signed off. Put it on your list of things to ask about before an offer — our guide to checking a house’s permit history before you buy walks through how to work a flag like that.

For HVAC, one more check beats the rest when the record is thin: the data plate on the unit itself. The serial number on the plate holds the production date for most makes — the outdoor plate is usually on the side or back panel near the refrigerant lines, and the furnace plate is usually inside the access cabinet. And the plate gives the build date, not the install date: a plate that says 2018 and a permit that says 2019 is the same unit, built one year and put in the next.

How much life is left once you have the date?

Subtract the age from normal life, and hold the answer loosely. Life ranges are guides, not guarantees — InterNACHI says its figures rest on regular maintenance and normal wear, not extreme weather, neglect, or overuse.

Asphalt shingles (3-tab) 20 years, asphalt (architectural) 30 years, metal 40 to 80 years, wood 25 years; hot climates drastically reduce asphalt shingle life, and hail, tornadoes, and hurricanes can shorten a roof’s life overall

Normal life for the roof — United States · InterNACHI Standard Estimated Life Expectancy Chart for Homes, checked November 9, 2026

Source: InterNACHI, Standard Estimated Life Expectancy Chart for Homes · Date pulled: November 9, 2026

A roof replaced in 2015 with 3-tab asphalt shingles is about 11 years old against a 20-year normal life — roughly half gone, with a fair few years left if it was put on right. The same 2015 roof in architectural shingles is about 11 against 30 — still young by that chart. Hot sun cuts the other way: InterNACHI warns that hot climates drastically reduce asphalt shingle life. In Phoenix or South Florida, plan on the low end of any range.

Air conditioner (central) 7 to 15 years, furnace 15 to 25 years, heat pump 10 to 15 years, boiler 40 years, conventional water heater 6 to 12 years

Normal life for the heating and cooling system — United States · InterNACHI Standard Estimated Life Expectancy Chart for Homes, checked November 9, 2026

Source: InterNACHI, Standard Estimated Life Expectancy Chart for Homes · Date pulled: November 9, 2026

HVAC ages faster than roofs. A central air conditioner that went in with a 2012 change-out is 14 years old against a 7-to-15-year range — plan for it now, not later. A furnace from the same year is 14 against 15 to 25 — older, but the horizon is years, not months. A heat pump from 2016 is about 10 against 10 to 15, and it works all year, so it builds hours faster than a summer-only air conditioner.

Your heat pump or air conditioner is more than 10 years old, or your furnace or boiler is more than 15 years old — consider replacing it; frequent repairs and rising energy bills also signal equipment has become less efficient

The planning ages ENERGY STAR uses — United States · ENERGY STAR replacement guidance, checked November 9, 2026

Source: ENERGY STAR, When is it time to replace? · Date pulled: November 9, 2026

ENERGY STAR uses the same ages as planning signals, not deadlines: think about replacing a heat pump or air conditioner past 10 years, or a furnace or boiler past 15, above all when repairs keep coming and the bills keep rising. A unit past those ages with a stack of repair lines in its history is a budget item to price into an offer.

What if there is no roof or HVAC permit at all?

Four honest answers, and only the fourth is a problem with the seller. First, the records may not go back far enough online. Some portals started a few years ago, and the paper years sit in a filing room. LegalClarity warns that older permits, above all those issued before a jurisdiction went digital, may not appear, and a home built before the 1990s with no permits at all may simply predate the digital system.

Second, the job may not have needed one where it happened. North Carolina is one clear example: the state exempts a lot of work costing $40,000 or less on a house from permits, including replacing roofing — unless it touches load-bearing structure, changes plumbing, or adds or replaces HVAC or electrical equipment. That split is North Carolina law — check your own city and county before you borrow it.

Third, the job may have been a repair, and repairs mostly leave no line. A new fan motor, a coil cleaning, a patched slope — these keep old systems running and they do not show up as replacements. That is the most common reason a house with an old roof shows no replacement line.

Fourth, the work may have been done with no permit. That is the case to take seriously. If the listing brags about a new roof and the permit list shows nothing at all — no re-roof, no repair, no inspection — ask for the invoice and the contractor’s name before you offer. If the building department cannot find it and the seller has no paperwork either, price the risk.

A plain routine for dating both systems

Settle the address first, with the parcel number if you have it. Permit databases are picky about spelling and street forms, and one empty search can mean a clean record or a mistyped address. Run the address, then the parcel number.

Pull the full list, newest first, and write down every line with the words roof, re-roof, mechanical, HVAC, furnace, air conditioner, heat pump, water heater, or change-out. Do not stop at the first roof line you see — the newest replacement sets the age. Then read each description and sort it: replacement or repair, roof or HVAC, furnace or condenser. Mark the newest replacement in each pile and write its final inspection date next to it, with the issue date as your backup. If a line is expired, circle it and ask about it — do not date anything from it.

Do the age math in the open. Roof: year now minus final year, against about 20 for 3-tab asphalt and 30 for architectural, less in hot sun. Air conditioner: against 7 to 15, plan past 10. Furnace: against 15 to 25, plan past 15. Heat pump: 10 to 15, and remember it works both seasons.

Then cross-check with your eyes and the plates. Curled or missing shingles on a “new” roof is a question, not a verdict. On the HVAC side, read the data plate serial on the outdoor unit and the furnace, and see if the build year lines up with the permit year. A plate a year or two older than the permit is normal. A plate ten years older than the permit’s “new system” claim is a problem.

Finish by writing it plainly in your offer notes: “Roof last replaced 2015, final inspection 2015, 3-tab asphalt, about 11 years old against a 20-year normal life. Furnace changed out 2019, condenser changed out 2014, air conditioner near its planning age.” That sentence lets you price a house instead of guessing at it. For the full one-address search, our guide to checking a house’s permit history before you buy covers the steps in order.

Frequently asked questions

Can permit history tell me exactly how old a roof is?

Not exactly, but it gets close. The newest closed re-roof or replacement line gives you the best public date for the roof. It cannot tell you the roof’s condition today — that takes an inspector, not a record.

What permit wording counts as a new roof, and what does not?

Re-roof, roof replacement, tear-off and re-roof, and new roof count. Roof repair, leak repair, patch, flashing, and partial-slope work do not — they are upkeep on an existing roof.

Is a mechanical permit the same as a new HVAC system?

Not always. Read the description: change-out, replace furnace, replace AC, new HVAC system, or new heat pump mean a new system. Service call, capacitor, blower motor, and coil cleaning mean a repair. Split the furnace from the condenser — one date does not cover both.

Which date should I use — the day the permit was issued or the final inspection?

The final inspection date, when the record has one. It is the day the city signed off that the finished work passed. Use the issue date only when no final date exists, and treat it as softer. Never date a system from an expired line.

What if there is no roof or HVAC permit for a house?

It proves only that no replacement was recorded. Maybe the work predates the online records. Maybe it never needed a permit, or it was only a repair — or somebody did it with no permit at all. Check the seller’s invoices, read the HVAC data plate, and ask the building department before you decide which it is.

How else can I check the age of an HVAC system?

Read the data plate on the unit. The serial number holds the production date for most makes — the outdoor plate is usually on the side or back panel near the refrigerant lines, and the furnace plate is usually inside the access cabinet. The model number will not date the unit.
